This verse states that the Qur'an is a Book sent down to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ so that he may bring people out of darkness into light, by the permission of their Lord, onto the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy. The commentators agree that darkness and light are metaphors for disbelief and faith. Al-Tabari explains that this bringing out happens through the call to the Qur'an, with God's guidance and kindness, and he takes the attribution of the act to the Prophet as evidence that people have a real acquisition of their deeds, while creation and direction belong to God, a position he sets against those who deny divine decree. Ibn Kathir stresses that guidance belongs to God alone, who guides whom He has decreed to be guided through His messenger.

Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that 'by the permission of their Lord' is borrowed from the lifting of a veil, meaning facilitation and divine support. Others take it to mean command, knowledge or will. As for the darkness, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada read it as misguidance and the light as guidance, while others take it as doubt and certainty, or innovation and sunna; these meanings are close and need not exclude one another. Al-Razi observes that unbelief is likened to darkness because it is the extreme of bewilderment, and faith to light because it makes the path clear.

The commentators also agree that the Prophet's mission is addressed to all of humanity, and that the Qur'an, though in Arabic, was revealed in the language of his people so that it could be understood. They conclude that those who prefer the present life to the Hereafter and turn others away from God's path face a severe punishment.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms God's ownership of everything in the heavens and on earth and warns the disbelievers of a severe punishment. On the reading of the word "Allah", al-Tabari records two well-known readings, one in the nominative and one in the genitive, and judges that both carry the same meaning, so he does not choose between them. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' understood the genitive as a reordering of the phrase, while al-Kisa'i saw it as one continuous sentence in which the words agree with one another. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi mainly stress that the name refers to the Lord who has absolute possession of creation. As for the word "wayl", al-Tabari takes it to be a valley in hell fed by the pus of its people, while others, such as Ibn 'Atiyya, read it as a plain expression of ruin. Al-Zamakhshari links the severe punishment to the wailing of the guilty. The verses that follow describe those who prefer the present life to the hereafter, who turn people away from God's path, and who seek to make it crooked. Most exegetes take preferring this world to mean actively choosing it, while al-Razi lays out a progression from going astray, to leading others astray, to attacking the path with doubts. All agree that this error is deep and far from the truth.

This verse describes those who prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter, who turn people away from the path of God, and who seek to make that path crooked so that it suits their desires. The commentators explain that 'prefer' (yastahibbuna) means to choose and give priority, and that the verb implies a deliberate effort which pushes love beyond its natural limit. They broadly agree that 'turning away from the path of God' means preventing people from believing and entering Islam, the path being the religion and law brought by the Prophet. The meaning of 'crooked' (ʿiwajan) is where opinions diverge. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as distorting and disparaging God's way; Ibn Abbas takes it as rejecting any religion other than Islam in Mecca; al-Suddi takes it as wishing harm upon the Prophet; al-Zamakhshari understands them to seek a flaw in this path in order to criticise it; and others attach the pronoun to the life of this world, meaning they pursue it by unlawful means. Al-Sha'rawi presents these attitudes as three degrees of error: preferring the present life, turning others away, and then distorting the doctrine. On grammar, Abu Hayyan rejects making 'those who' a qualifier of the disbelievers, since it would separate the adjective from its noun with an unrelated phrase. All agree that 'a far-off error' is a figure of speech, since the one who strays is the one who is far, and that this error is deep and hard to leave without God's help.

This verse states that God sent no messenger except in the language of his own people, so that he could make the message clear to them. The commentators explain that guidance and misguidance rest with God alone: He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.

Most exegetes agree on the purpose of this arrangement: to make the message understood and to establish proof, so that no one can claim ignorance. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir present it as a constant divine practice. Ibn Kathir adds that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was given a universal mission to all people, while earlier prophets were sent to their own nations. Az-Zamakhshari argues that revelation in Arabic, the language of the Prophet's people, was more precise and less open to distortion and dispute, and that translation then carried the message to other nations.

On the words « God leads astray whom He wills », Sunni commentators such as al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari take them to mean that both misguidance and guidance come from God. The Mu'tazilites, represented by az-Zamakhshari, read misguidance as God leaving a person without help and withholding grace, and guidance as granting grace and support. Al-Razi rejects this reading and answers their arguments at length. He also notes that the verb is in the indicative, which some take to mark a new sentence rather than a continuation of 'to make clear'.

The commentators differ on who 'their people' refers to. Al-Dahhak was reported to say it refers to the Prophet ﷺ, that all scriptures were revealed in Arabic and then rendered into each nation's tongue. Az-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan reject this view, since it would imply that the Torah was revealed in Arabic to explain things to the Arabs, which they regard as an unsound meaning.

In this verse God says that He sent Moses with His signs and commanded him to bring his people out of the darkness of ignorance and disbelief into the light of faith, and to remind them of the Days of God. The commentators agree that the phrase «Days of God» carries two related meanings. The first is God's blessings upon the Children of Israel, such as their rescue from Pharaoh's people, the parting of the sea, the shading cloud, and the manna and quails, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir. The second is God's retributions upon earlier nations, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, as held by Muqatil, Ibn Zayd and al-Razi. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi combined both meanings, and Ibn 'Atiyya held that the word covers both, since reminding can be done through either. Some philologists cited a line of 'Amr ibn Kulthum to show that the days can mean blessings, but al-Tabari rejected this proof, arguing that the long days in the line refer to the severity of battles. As for darkness and light, most take them as misguidance and guidance, or disbelief and faith, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur also include polytheism and disobedience. On the closing phrase about every patient, grateful person, Qatada explains that the believer is patient in trial and grateful in ease, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the report that faith is half patience and half gratitude. Some add that the verse addresses every believer, since patience and gratitude mark the believer, as al-Mawardi and al-Baydawi state.

This verse records Moses telling his people, the Children of Israel, to remember God's favour in rescuing them from Pharaoh's people, who subjected them to terrible torment, slaughtered their sons and spared their women, and he adds that this was a great trial from their Lord. The commentators note that the conjunction before 'slaughtering' marks it as a further form of torment added to the general suffering, whereas in the verses of al-Baqara and al-A'raf the verb without the conjunction explains the torment itself. Most agree that 'sparing' the women means letting them live, and al-Tabari cites the hadith 'kill the elders of the polytheists and spare their young' to illustrate the word. The meaning of 'trial' is debated: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan take it to mean a blessing, al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani take it as a test or hardship, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue it can mean both, since trials come through good and evil alike. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur see the reference as both the suffering they endured and the deliverance from it. Regarding 'He announced', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as informing, and Ibn Kathir also considers the sense of swearing an oath. Most commentators make gratitude the cause of increase: al-Hasan understands it as greater obedience, Ibn 'Abbas as greater reward, and al-Rabi' as greater bounty, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the increase may be in worldly goods as well as in the hereafter. All agree that God needs nothing from His servants' gratitude, and that the threat of severe punishment for ingratitude balances the promise made to the thankful.

This verse records that God, through Moses, informed the Children of Israel that if they were grateful for His favours through faith and obedience, He would increase them, and if they denied them, His punishment would be severe. The commentators agree that gratitude brings increase, but they differ on what that increase is and what gratitude is directed at. Al-Tabari, al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Rabi' take the object of gratitude to be God's favour, with the increase being further bounty or obedience, while Ibn 'Abbas explains gratitude as monotheism and obedience, the increase being a greater reward. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the increase as further blessings in this world, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya reports scholars who restrict it to the Hereafter, while himself finding it possible that it covers both worlds.

On the word kufr, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it to mean denying and being ungrateful for the favours, al-Razi specifying ingratitude. Ibn Juzayy allows that it may mean ingratitude or disbelief, preferring the first because it is set against gratitude. Al-Razi defines gratitude as acknowledging a benefactor's favour with reverence, and distinguishes spiritual from material blessings. The commentaries also mention David's words to God about gratitude and a saying attributed to the Prophet, without drawing any legal ruling from them.

The commentators explain that Moses tells his people that if you, and all who are on earth, reject the favours of God, this will not harm Him: He is self-sufficient, needing no thanks from His creatures, and worthy of praise in His essence even if no one praises Him. Most of them agree that the harm of disbelief falls on the disbeliever himself. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir stress that ingratitude does not diminish God's dominion in any way. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi add that wealth and praiseworthiness are essential attributes of God, neither increased by gratitude nor reduced by denial. There is a difference over the meaning of kufr: some take it as denying God's favours, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya also allow that it means disbelief in the Oneness of God. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that gratitude benefits only the one who shows it, and that God promises more to the thankful and punishment to the ungrateful. Abu Hayyan supplies the unstated answer to the conditional as: the harm of your disbelief will fall on you. Al-Alusi and al-Qasimi observe that praise is owed to beneficence, so even those who reject God in effect praise Him through the favours they receive. Several commentators draw from the verse the lesson that worship adds nothing to God and benefits only the worshipper.

This verse from Surah Ibrahim recalls that messengers came to earlier peoples, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, bringing clear proofs. Their peoples responded by putting their hands to their mouths, then declaring that they rejected what they had been sent with and were in troubling doubt about what they were called to. The commentators differ on the meaning of this gesture. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari take it to mean they bit their fingers in rage at the messengers, citing the verse about biting the fingertips in anger in Al 'Imran; al-Tabari judges this the most sound. Ibn 'Abbas holds that they were astonished at God's Book and put their hands to their mouths, while Abu Salih understands a sign to be silent. Mujahid and Qatada say they rejected the messengers' words and denied them with their mouths, a reading Ibn Kathir finds supported by the next clause. Al-Hasan says they placed their hands on the messengers' mouths to stop them speaking. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash read it as an image of refusing to answer. Al-Zamakhshari prefers the sense of discouraging the messengers from being believed. Some read the 'hands' as blessings, a view reported from al-Zajjaj and al-Farra'. On the claim to be disbelievers yet in doubt, al-Razi explains that they meant that if they were not outright unbelievers, they were at least doubtful. As for the unknown generations, Ibn Mas'ud said the genealogists lie, Ibn 'Abbas spoke of thirty unknown forefathers between 'Adnan and Isma'il, and al-Razi holds that the verse denies knowing their very identities.

The commentators explain that the messengers answer their doubting peoples with a rhetorical question of reproach: how can there be doubt about God, Creator of the heavens and the earth, that is, their Originator and Fashioner? They then call the people to faith so that God may forgive some of their sins and grant them respite until an appointed term. The peoples reply that the messengers are only humans like themselves, that they wish to turn them away from what their fathers worshipped, and they demand a clear authority. The exegetes agree on the general meaning: affirming God's oneness and power, with the question being rhetorical. They differ on the nature of the doubt: al-Qatada took it to concern God's oneness, others concern obedience, and al-Mawardi also considers divine power. On the particle 'min' in 'some of your sins': Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash held it to be superfluous, which Sibawayh rejected, reading it as partitive; al-Zamakhshari read it as partitive, limiting forgiveness to what lies between the servant and God rather than wrongs against people, while al-Razi rejected most of these readings. As for the 'appointed term', the Mu'tazilites spoke of two possible terms, whereas Sunni scholars hold that there is one fixed term. Ibn 'Abbas understood it as enjoyment of good things until death. The 'clear authority' the peoples demand is for some a stubborn demand for a miracle, and for others a denial that a human could be sent as a messenger at all. The messengers reply that they are indeed human, but that God bestows His favour on whom He wills, and that no sign comes except by God's permission.

This verse records the messengers' reply to their peoples: they concede that they are human beings like them, yet affirm that God bestows His favour on whomever He wills among His servants, and that bringing a clear proof is not in their power but depends on God's permission; therefore the believers should put their trust in God alone. The commentators agree that sharing humanity does not imply equality in every respect, and that prophethood is a gift from God. On the meaning of favour, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as guidance and success, while al-Baghawi, al-Sam'ani, al-Nasafi and al-Mahalli take it to mean prophethood; al-Qurtubi cites Sahl ibn Abd Allah, who explains it as the recitation of the Qur'an and understanding its meaning. Regarding sultan, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn read it as proof or argument, whereas al-Mawardi lists three senses: the Book, proof, and miracle. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur note that the messengers first grant their opponents' premise and then correct the conclusion, a known dialectical method. On the repetition of the command to trust in God, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the first mention establishes trust and the second calls for steadfastness in it. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan observe that the messengers swear to endure the harm inflicted upon them. The threat of expulsion or return to their religion is discussed by al-Baghawi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir, who report that God answered with the destruction of the wrongdoers and the settling of the prophets' community in the land.

The verse records the messengers' reply to their people, who threatened them: why should we not put our trust in God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will patiently bear the harm you inflict on us, and the believers must rely on God alone. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi, agree that this means relying on God, persevering in the call and bearing hurt patiently, and they note that trust is an act of the heart that does not exclude taking the means. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read the first call to trust as the beginning of this attitude and the second as steadfastness in it. Al-Razi explains that the prophets trust God because they know the disbelievers cannot harm them without His permission. On the word for paths, al-Zajjaj and al-Nasafi take it as the lawful way to follow, while Ibn al-Jawzi understands it as the clarification of right guidance or the way of trust. As for the unbelievers' threat to expel the messengers or force them back into their religion, al-Tabari takes the particle 'or' to mean 'unless' or 'until', while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand 'return' as 'becoming'. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Tha'alibi report God's promise to destroy the wrongdoers and settle the believers in the land, a promise for those who fear standing before Him and His threat; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take that standing as the reckoning, while al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj read it as divine watchfulness. The commentators present the passage as a lesson for believers to remain firm in the truth and not be shaken by the threats of those who reject it.

This verse reports the threat of the disbelievers to their messengers: they will expel them from their land or they must return to their religion. God then reveals to His messengers that He will destroy the wrongdoers and settle them in the land after them. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Razi, agree that it is a promise of victory and a good end for the prophets and for those who fear God's standing and His threat. Al-Tabari explains that "return" means entering their religion, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold that the word here means "become", a common usage in Arabic, which does not imply that the prophets ever followed the disbelievers' religion. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that "aw" may mean "unless" or "until", but he finds the sense of choice more fitting. Al-Tabari takes the punishment to target the polytheists, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya argues that only those who persist in wrongdoing are meant. On the word "maqam", al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zajjaj take it as the place of standing on the Day of Judgment, al-Farra' as God's watchful oversight of deeds, and al-Razi offers several other readings. The overall meaning is that God supports His messengers and gives them the land, as He did for earlier prophets.

This verse reports the threat of the disbelieving peoples to their messengers: they would either expel them from their land or make them return to their religion. God answers that He will destroy the wrongdoers, and then settle the messengers and those who followed them in the land after those people. This is the reward for those who fear standing before Him and dread His warning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand "the land" as the land of the wrongdoers and their homes, and Qatada explains the promise as victory in this world and Paradise in the next, citing verses such as "We caused the people who had been deemed weak to inherit the eastern and western parts of the earth."

The commentators agree that the promise is addressed to the messengers and their companions, and that the destruction of one party and the settlement of another follow the divine pattern of granting victory to the prophets. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur explain "my station" (maqam) as the place of standing for judgement on the Day of Resurrection, or as God's watch over deeds, or as an emphatic addition with no separate meaning. Al-Farra' takes it as a verbal noun whose subject is God, while al-Akhfash reads it as a reference to punishment.

Opinions differ on the phrase "or you will return to our creed". Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain that "return" here means "become", since the messengers never held that creed, while al-Razi adds that the opponents were acting on their mistaken assumption. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that "or" may mean "until" or "unless", and Ibn 'Atiyya considers that reading weak.

The verse says that the messengers sought victory from their Lord against peoples who threatened to expel them from their land or force them back into their religion. They were granted victory, and every arrogant tyrant hostile to the truth was ruined. Commentators differ on who is asking for victory. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, followed by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, take it to be the messengers seeking help from God. Ibn Zayd, al-Qurtubi and others take it to be the peoples themselves, who asked for a punishment, as the Quraysh did when they said, 'If this is the truth from You, rain down stones upon us from the sky.' Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan allow a sarcastic reading by the disbelievers, or that both sides are meant. On the word jabbar, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it to mean the proud man who turns from the truth, Qatada the one who refuses to say there is no god but God, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi link it to arrogance toward obedience to God. All agree that 'anid is one who opposes the truth and turns away from it. On the phrase 'behind him is Hell', al-Tabari, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qurtubi understand 'behind' as 'in front of', while Ibn al-Anbari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur take it as 'after him'. The sadid is, for Mujahid and Qatada, pus and blood, and for Muhammad ibn Ka'b the runoff from the bodies of the damned. Finally, death coming from every place is read by most as causes of death surrounding him, or as pains in every part of the body, yet he does not die, according to Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari.

This verse describes the fate of the arrogant obstinate tyrant after his death: Hell lies ahead of him, as most commentators explain the word "from behind him", and he is given to drink a liquid of pus and blood. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that "he gulps it" means he drinks it sip by sip because of its bitterness and heat, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan understand "he can hardly swallow it" to mean that he does not even come close to swallowing it. Al-Razi notes that swallowing may occur after great effort, yet without any pleasure or acceptance. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari say death comes to him from every place, that is from every part of his body according to Ibrahim al-Taymi, and al-Baghawi says this means the pain and anguish of death, while al-Akhfash takes it to mean the trials that afflict the disbeliever in the Fire. He does not die, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak say, because his soul stays stuck in his throat. Most commentators take the "severe punishment" to mean eternal dwelling in the Fire or a torment harsher than what came before, while al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad takes it to mean the stifling of breath within the bodies. The commentators differ on who is meant by "they sought victory": Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say the messengers who asked God for victory, Ibn Zayd says the disbelievers who asked for the punishment, and Ibn Kathir leans toward including both. A few relate the passage to the people of Mecca in the years of drought, a view most commentators do not adopt.

This verse likens the deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord to ashes that a violent wind scatters on a stormy day, leaving nothing that can be gathered. The commentators agree that these deeds, including good ones such as keeping family ties, feeding guests and freeing captives, will bring no benefit on the Day of Resurrection, because they were not built on faith and were not done purely for God, and disbelief has annulled them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress that these people hoped for a reward they will not find. Al-Razi holds that the annulment covers both deeds done for God and deeds done for idols, since neither remains. On grammar, Sibawayh takes the word 'mathal' as a subject whose predicate is implied, meaning 'in what is recited to you', while al-Farra' supposes an omitted noun, 'the likeness of the deeds of those who disbelieved'. Ibn 'Atiyya and others make 'their deeds' a second subject whose predicate is 'like ashes'. As for 'a stormy day', the commentators offer several readings: the adjective refers to the day, since the wind occurs in it, or it refers to the wind, with the noun implied, or it is an adjective of the wind itself that took the case of the preceding noun. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the 'far error' is the total loss of reward. Al-Qurtubi adds that the phrase expresses a distance from the path of salvation.

This verse tells us that God created the heavens and the earth with truth, meaning with wisdom and a sound purpose and not in vain, and that by reflecting on this great creation one should recognise that He is able, if He wills, to remove the people and bring a new creation, which is not beyond Him. The commentators agree that the address is to the Prophet, peace be upon him, while its intended audience is his community, and some extend it to anyone fit to hear it, with the verb 'see' meaning knowledge gained through reflection. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note that the two readings, 'khalaqa' and 'khaliq', are both well transmitted, close in meaning, and both acceptable. As for the 'new creation', al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi understand it as a different people more obedient to God, whereas Ibn Kathir takes it as resurrection after annihilation, a view Ibn Sa'di considers likely given what follows about the Day of Judgement. Al-Zamakhshari explains that nothing is beyond God because He is powerful in His very essence, a claim that others criticise sharply. Ibn Ashur sees the verse as a bridge showing how easily God can destroy a mighty people, and al-Razi sets out several senses of 'truth', one in the Sunni view as evidence of the Creator's knowledge and power, and one in the Mu'tazili view as the negation of vanity.

The commentators explain that this verse states that God, who created the heavens and the earth with truth, meaning not in vain, can if He wills destroy you and bring a new creation in your place, and that this is neither impossible nor difficult for Him. They agree that the word 'azīz here means hard, difficult or unattainable, and they see in the verse a reminder of the greatness of God's power. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud report that the address is to the disbelievers of Mecca, and that the 'new creation' means a people more obedient to God. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di also consider that destruction followed by resurrection in a new creation is possible, relying on what follows about the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari holds that God is powerful by His essence and is not restricted to one object over another, so that an act occurs as soon as the will arises and no obstacle stands in the way; Al-Alusi and Ibn Kathir object that this explanation departs from Sunni doctrine. On the reading, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi report that most readers recite 'khalaqa' in the past tense, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'khāliq'. Al-Tabari considers both readings well established and close in meaning. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that the phrase 'bi-l-haqq' is read by Sunnis as proof of the Creator's existence and power, and by Mu'tazilis as the negation of vanity. In sum, the verse affirms God's complete power, and the disagreements concern the addressees, the meaning of the new creation, and the account of that power.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when all people come out before God. The weak, meaning the followers, say to the arrogant, meaning their leaders, that they followed them in this world and ask whether they can take away any part of God's punishment from them. The leaders reply that if God had guided them, they would have guided their followers, and conclude that patience and impatience are equal, since there is no escape for them. On the meaning of 'coming out', al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi explain it as rising from the graves, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as being exposed before God, since the sinners had thought their hidden acts were concealed from Him. The commentators agree that the weak are the followers and the arrogant are the leaders. They differ on the phrase 'if God had guided us'. Ibn Abbas and al-Wahidi take it as an admission that the leaders misled others, al-Zamakhshari holds that they are lying and blame God, while others read it as referring to the path of salvation from punishment. Several reports, including one from Muqatil and one from Mohammed ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, describe the damned alternating between patience and lamentation for long periods without benefit, though al-Tabari considers the chain weak. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi link this exchange to Hell itself. All commentators explain 'mahis' as a refuge or a way of escape.

This verse records what Satan will say to his followers on the Day of Resurrection, after the judgment has been settled, with the people of Paradise in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire. He acknowledges that God's promise of resurrection and reward was a true promise, while his own promise denying these things was false, so he betrayed them. The commentators explain that he had no compelling power or proof over them: he only called them, and they answered of their own accord. He therefore tells them to blame themselves rather than him, says that he cannot help them and they cannot help him, and disowns their having associated him with God in obedience. The verse ends with a warning of painful punishment for the wrongdoers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi agree on the general meaning and that the address is to the damned, the lesson being to warn the listeners. They differ on timing: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir place the speech after the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, while others place it during the reckoning. On the meaning of 'authority', most take it as proof or argument, while others take it as force; Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di add that Satan's power is only to incite those who freely follow him. Commentators also debate human responsibility: al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Qayyim take the verse as evidence of free choice, while Ash'arite theologians read it through the doctrine of acquisition (kasb) under divine will. On the linguistic side, Hamza's reading 'bi-musrikhiyya' with a kasra was criticised by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, defended by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', and attributed by Qutrub to the dialect of the Banu Yarbu'.

This verse describes the entry of those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever by the permission of their Lord, and where their greeting will be peace. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the greeting is peace, and the abode is eternal. They differ on who gives the greeting. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the believers greet one another and that the angels greet them as well. Al-Baghawi, al-Sam'ani and al-Razi also mention that God Himself may be the one who greets them, and al-Razi adds that the Merciful Lord greets them with this word. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the phrase by the permission of their Lord connects either to the entry or, in one reading, to the angels' greeting. Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi take it that the angels bring them in by God's leave. Al-Razi notes that peace implies safety from the afflictions of this world. The verse follows Satan's speech, in which he disowns his followers after the judgment. The commentators then link the passage to the parable of the good word, which al-Tabari and most of his sources identify with the palm tree, supported by a hadith from Ibn Umar. Others take it to mean faith, the testimony of faith, or the believer himself.

This verse offers an image of a good word compared to a blessed tree. Most commentators take the good word to be the testimony that there is no god but God, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj understand it as faith itself, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas and 'Atiyya al-'Awfi as the believer himself. The tree is, for most, the date palm, as reported from the Prophet through Ibn 'Umar and Anas, though Ibn 'Abbas says it is a tree in Paradise, and Ibn 'Atiyya holds it may be any tree with these qualities. Its rooted base stands for firm faith, its branches rising to heaven for the elevation of good deeds, and its fruit for the blessings that follow. Al-Tabari concludes that the phrase 'every season' means all times, since the image must not contradict what it represents, yet the scholars differ on the length of the season: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Mujahid say a year, al-Hasan and Qatada six months, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab two months, and Ibn 'Abbas elsewhere each morning and evening. Al-Razi expands the image into the beauty, stability and constant fruit of knowing God, and Ibn al-Qayyim takes the root to be knowledge and conviction, the branches deeds, and the fruit good effects. The contrasting evil word, the word of disbelief, is likened to a bitter tree, usually identified as the colocynth, uprooted and without any stability.

In this verse God compares the good word, which most commentators take to be the declaration of faith or faith itself, to a goodly tree whose root is firmly fixed in the earth and whose branches reach up to heaven, giving its fruit at every season by the permission of its Lord. The commentators explain the good word in several ways: the testimony that there is no god but God, faith, or the believer himself. As for the tree, most identify it as the date palm, relying on reports from the Prophet transmitted through Ibn Umar and Anas, while Ibn Abbas describes it as a tree in Paradise. Al-Tabari holds the palm to be the most correct view because of the soundness of the prophetic report. On the meaning of 'hin', opinions differ: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrima say a year or six months, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab says two months, and Ibn Abbas, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others say every morning and evening, which al-Tabari prefers because the believer's deeds rise every day. Al-Razi and others stress that the firmness, height and constant yield of the tree express the rootedness of faith, the ascent of good works and the lasting blessing that follows. The passage concludes that such comparisons bring abstract truths closer to the mind, so that reflection and remembrance are encouraged.

In this verse God gives a parable of the evil word, meaning the word of disbelief and associating partners with God, likening it to an evil tree that yields nothing good, uprooted from the surface of the earth with no firm root and no stability. The commentators agree that the point is that disbelief has no firm foundation for the disbeliever to rest on, and that no righteous deed rises from him to God. They differ on the identity of the tree. Anas ibn Malik, Mujahid, and Ibn Abbas in one report, as well as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most scholars, say it is the bitter colocynth (handhal), and a hadith in al-Tirmidhi reports this, though al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the stopped version (a saying of Anas) is more authoritative, as al-Tirmidhi himself said. Others mention garlic, dodder, truffle, or algae. Ibn Abbas also reports that it is a tree never created on earth. Ibn Atiyya holds that it refers to an unspecified tree possessing these traits. The word ijtuttat means completely uprooted, and ma laha min qarar means it has no stability. Al-Zamakhshari and others draw the lesson that a word without proof is fragile and cannot endure.

This verse states that God firmly establishes the believers through the firm word, the declaration of faith in God and His Messenger, both in this life and in the Hereafter. Commentators differ on what the two lives mean. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi mainly hold that the worldly life is the span of a person's life and the Hereafter is the questioning in the grave, when two angels ask the deceased about his Lord, his religion and his prophet; the believer answers rightly and God makes him steadfast, a view supported by hadiths from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib. Tawus and Qatada instead take the worldly life to be the time of questioning in the grave and the Hereafter to be the Day of Resurrection, and Qatada adds that the steadfastness in this life comes through good deeds. Al-Zamakhshari reads the steadfastness in this life as firmness in faith under trials, and in the Hereafter as composure when questioned at the Gathering. The second part means that God leads astray the wrongdoers, meaning the polytheists, who fail to give the right answer, as Ibn 'Ashur and al-Sha'rawi note. The verse ends with the words that God does what He wills, meaning that guidance and misguidance rest on His will and wisdom, and no one may question Him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the tomb interpretation, while al-Razi links the steadfastness to the constancy of belief during life.

This verse speaks of people who exchanged Allah's blessing for disbelief. The commentators explain that the blessing is the sending of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ among them with his religion, and that changing it into disbelief means rejecting and denying his message, or replacing gratitude with ingratitude. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, take the people to be the polytheists of Quraysh, and understand the "abode of ruin" as Hell, which they will enter. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Mujahid and Qatada instead refer to those killed at Badr, or to the battle of Badr itself, and Ibn Atiyya treats "Jahannam" as an explanatory apposition. Umar and Ali report that the two wicked branches of Quraysh were the Banu al-Mughira and the Banu Umayya, while Ibn Abbas, in one report, applies the verse to Jabala ibn al-Ayham, who had converted to Christianity; Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir note that Ibn Abbas did not mean the verse was revealed about him, but that it applies to anyone who does the same. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi offer two readings: the turning of gratitude into disbelief, or the loss of the blessing with disbelief taking its place. Several commentators observe that the verb "to lead astray" may carry the sense of consequence, and that the command "enjoy yourselves" is a threat rather than a permission. All conclude that their destination is the Fire.

The commentators explain that this verse, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, marvels at those who exchanged God's blessing for ingratitude, replacing thankfulness with disbelief, and who brought their people down to the abode of ruin, which is Hell, where they will burn, and what a wretched dwelling it is. Most agree that the reference is to the Quraysh of Mecca who rejected the Prophet after God sent him among them, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir take the abode of ruin to be Hell in the afterlife, following Ibn Zayd, while Ali, Mujahid and Ata ibn Yasar hold that it refers to the place where the dead of Badr fell, so that Hell is an explanatory apposition or the object of a verb implied. Umar and Ali reported that the phrase designates two clans of the Quraysh, the Banu Umayya and the Banu al-Mughira, one of whom was destroyed at Badr and the other granted respite. Ibn Abbas also named Jabala ibn al-Ayham and his followers among the Arabs who joined the Byzantines, though al-Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan clarify that he did not mean the verse was revealed about them, only that it applies to anyone who acts likewise. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read the verb with a fatha on the ya, making misguidance a consequence rather than a purpose, while the other readers use a damma. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the command to enjoy this life is a warning rather than a permission.

This verse describes those who exchanged God's blessing for ingratitude, who for most commentators are the Quraysh of Mecca. They set up rivals to God, idols they worshipped, in order to lead people astray from His path. The Prophet is told to say to them, as a threat: enjoy yourselves, for your final destination is the Fire. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the andad are partners or idols. The verb liyudillu can be read with a damma, meaning to lead others astray, or with a fatha, meaning that they lead themselves astray; this second reading, preferred by Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan, makes the lam one of consequence, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note. Al-Tabari holds that the command to enjoy is not a permission but a rebuke and a warning, a view shared by al-Jaza'iri. As to the occasion of revelation, most commentators point to the Quraysh; Ali and Umar relate it to the Banu Makhzum and the Banu Umayya, Ibn Abbas to Jabala ibn al-Ayham, and al-Hasan takes it as general to all polytheists. Ibn Kathir notes that the ruling applies to anyone who acts in the same way. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the abode of ruin is Hell, while others take it as the defeat at Badr. Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi stress that such enjoyment is brief and will not benefit its taker in the face of the eternal Fire.

The verse tells the Prophet to tell his believing servants to establish the prayer and to spend from what God has provided, secretly and openly, before a day comes on which there will be no trade and no friendship. Most commentators understand the secret and open giving as meaning what is hidden and what is visible, as al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report of the majority, while al-Qasim ibn Yahya, cited by al-Mawardi, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, holds that secret giving is voluntary and open giving is obligatory. Al-Mawardi offers a further possibility that secret refers to charity and open to general expenditure. Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understood the prayer as the five daily prayers and the spending as the zakat on wealth. Grammarians differ on why the verb is in the jussive. Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj invoke an implied imperative particle or condition, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan posit an omitted speech. As for the day without trade or friendship, Abu Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba and al-Tabari explain that trade means ransom and friendship means companionship. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur add that people usually spend for exchange or for favours, whereas spending for God alone will benefit on that day. Qatada, as quoted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, said that friendships not founded on God will end. The Qur'an readings differ between the nominative and the accusative for the two nouns. All commentators agree the day is the Day of Resurrection.

This verse states that God created the heavens and the earth, sends down water from the sky and brings forth fruits from it as sustenance for people, subjects the ships to sail the sea by His command, and subjects the rivers to them. Al-Tabari and Mujahid explain that the rivers are subjected in every city for the benefit of its people, while al-Farra' and al-Samani take the subjection to mean that they are made navigable so that people can direct them wherever they wish. The commentators agree that the verse enumerates God's favours in order to establish His oneness and His exclusive right to worship. Regarding the sun and the moon, most explain that they move tirelessly and serve human interests, with Ibn 'Abbas adding that their perseverance is obedience to God, while others understand that they never slow down. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi describe the alternation of night and day as serving livelihood and rest, whereas al-Razi considers the subjection of night and day a metaphor, since they are accidents. The phrase 'and He gave you of all that you asked Him' has been read in different ways: al-Akhfash and Ibn al-Anbari take 'min' as partitive or an omitted element, while others, following the tanwin reading, take 'ma' as a negation, meaning of what you did not ask, according to al-Dahhak. The verse concludes that man is wrongdoing and ungrateful. Ibn 'Abbas identifies him as Abu Jahl, while most exegetes understand the whole human species. The meaning of 'zalum' and 'kaffar' varies: the wrongdoer is the one who denies his benefactor's favour and thanks another, and the ungrateful one denies the favour; alternatively, the wrongdoer complains in hardship and the ungrateful one hoards and withholds in ease.

This verse recalls that God subjected the sun and the moon to the service of people, both moving constantly, and the night and day which alternate, the night for rest and the day for work and livelihood. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, explain 'constant' as meaning that the two keep moving and shining and bring about what suits the earth, bodies and plants, which is the most widespread reading. Al-Tabari also records, through Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil ibn Hayyan, that the constancy is in obedience to God. Ibn 'Atiyya finds this acceptable if obedience means submission to the subjection, but considers it remote if it means voluntary obedience like that of people, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Khazin accept it as a possible meaning. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that subjection means putting something at one's service and directing it, and that applied to night and day it is a metaphor, since they are accidents, as the theologians note. The list of favours serves to show that God alone is their author. The phrase 'He gave you of all you asked Him' is read by exegetes either with min as partitive, as intensive, or as meaning what you did not ask for. The verse concludes that people cannot count God's favours and that humanity is wrongdoing and ungrateful; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi present these as traits of human nature in general, without drawing any separate ruling.

This verse states that God has given people everything they asked of Him, that His blessings are too many to count, and that man is nevertheless a wrongdoer to himself and ungrateful to his Lord. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid read "of all that you asked Him" as meaning all that you desired, while others such as Dahhak and Qatada add that it includes what you did not ask for, such as the sun, the moon, the night and the day. Al-Tabari prefers the reading that joins "kull" to "ma". Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and other grammarians take "min" as partitive, with the second noun left implicit, whereas al-Farra' reads the sense as "if you had asked for it". On "you cannot count them", many commentators, including al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya, explain that the impossibility applies even to counting them, let alone thanking God for them, since a single blessing contains countless others. Regarding "zalum kaffar", most explain that the wrongdoer is one who thanks someone other than the true Benefactor and the ingrate one who denies the favour, while others see it as wronging oneself through disobedience and disbelief in the Lord. Ibn Abbas held that the verse refers to Abu Jahl, while al-Zajjaj took "man" as a generic term aimed chiefly at the disbeliever. Al-Sha'rawi adds that even what God withholds is a blessing.

Al-Tabari and most commentators explain that Ibrahim asked God to make Makkah a secure town, where its people and whoever enters it are safe, and to keep him and his descendants far from idol worship. Most define a sanam as a figured statue, while some define a wathan as an unshaped idol, although others do not make this distinction. The exegetes read the verb ijtinab as keeping away and as a request for steadfastness. Since Ibrahim is protected from sin, his prayer is understood as a request for greater protection, firmness and humility before God's favours. They agree that the sons refer to his direct offspring and that the prayer was answered for them, since none of his direct descendants worshipped an idol according to Mujahid and Ibn Kathir. Ibn 'Uyayna holds that no descendant of Isma'il worshipped an idol, the Arabs venerating stones set up and circled, which would not count as a sanam. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi argue that the supplication was general and granted only in part, a view al-Shinqiti supports by citing other verses. The statement that the idols misled many people is generally read figuratively, the idol being the cause of the error, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that real responsibility rests with the one who devised it. As for the words about whoever disobeys me, you are forgiving and merciful, Qatada and al-Suddi and Muqatil ibn Hayyan take it as sin short of shirk or disobedience followed by repentance, while others read it as a prayer made before he knew that God does not forgive associating partners with Him.

This verse is part of Abraham's supplication, peace be upon him. In it he says that idols led many people astray until they worshipped them, that whoever follows him in monotheism belongs to his religion, and that whoever disobeys him is left to God's forgiveness and mercy. The commentators agree that ascribing the misguidance to the idols is figurative, since they are lifeless objects that do nothing; people went astray because of them, as one says that worldly life deceived them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Abraham asked God to keep him and his offspring from worshipping idols, and they take his offspring to mean his direct descendants. Mujahid holds that none of them worshipped a statue, while Ibn 'Uyayna argues that the descendants of Ismail never worshipped an idol in the strict sense. On the closing words, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take the disobedient to be one who persists in associating partners with God, al-Suddi takes it to mean one who repents after disobeying, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan takes it to mean disobedience short of shirk. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari read it as an intercession for those guilty of major sins, whereas Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a simple entrusting of the matter to God's mercy, without asking forgiveness for polytheism. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Sa'di highlight Abraham's gentleness toward those who disobey.

Abraham, having settled his descendants, Isma'il and his mother Hajar, in a barren valley beside the Sacred House, asks God that they may establish prayer, that He incline the hearts of some people towards them, and that He provide them with fruits so that they may be thankful. The commentators agree that the valley is Mecca, and that calling the House sacred means that its sanctity is to be respected and that wrongdoing there is graver. Establishing prayer is presented as the chief purpose of the settlement. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others explain that the word « some » in « some of the people » indicates a part: had it said « the hearts of the people », Persians and Romans would have crowded there, according to Mujahid, and Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that only Muslims are meant. As for « incline », most take it to mean longing and yearning, others the desire to make the pilgrimage, and Ibn Abbas the desire to dwell in Mecca. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand that the fruits are brought in through trade, while Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari relay reports about a town of Syria being moved to Ta'if. Al-Baydawi notes that the request is not limited to believers. Most read the closing clause as gratitude to God for His favours, while some relate it to the gratitude of the inhabitants for an easy livelihood.

In this verse Abraham addresses his Lord, acknowledging that God knows what he conceals and what he displays, and that nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him. The commentators agree on the general meaning: God knows His servant's needs better than anyone, so the supplication is not meant to inform Him but to express servitude, humility and dependence on Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari all explain this, and al-Zamakhshari adds that the believer also shows eagerness to obtain God's favours. As for what Abraham concealed and displayed, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil take it to be his grief over Ishmael and his mother left in a valley without crops, al-Nakha'i takes it to be his love for them and his apparent harshness toward Sarah, while others see it as sorrow at the separation, weeping and prayer. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya report his exchange with Hajar at parting. On who speaks the phrase 'nothing is hidden from God', most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, take it as God's own words confirming Abraham's, while others attribute it to Abraham himself; al-Jubba'i sees it as a divine parenthesis. Most hold that 'min' signifies totality. Ibn 'Ashur regards the sentence as a concluding statement affirming the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge. The exegetes connect this verse with the rest of the supplication and with the praise that follows for the gift of Ishmael and Isaac in old age.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, praises God for granting him Isma'il and Ishaq in his old age, and affirms that his Lord is the One who hears supplication, meaning who answers it. The commentators explain the preposition 'upon' (ʿalā al-kibar) as meaning 'along with', that is, while he was old and had despaired of children, which makes the gift greater and sweeter. They agree that the verse is linked to the preceding prayer and is a thanksgiving for its answer. On the dates of the births, the reports differ. Ibn ʿAbbas, cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, says Isma'il was born when Ibrahim was ninety-nine and Ishaq when he was a hundred and twelve. Other figures are given, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr places the good news of Ishaq after a hundred and seventeen years. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the gift to cover both sons. Al-Razi notes that the praise may have come long after the first prayer, while another view makes the sentence a statement of God's own, since Ishaq had not yet been born when Ibrahim left Hagar and Isma'il in Mecca. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari, explain that 'hearing' means accepting and answering, and that supplication may refer either to a request or to worship. The commentators draw no legal ruling from this verse.

Abraham asks his Lord to make him steadfast in establishing the prayer, with its proper pillars and limits, and to grant the same to some of his descendants. He then asks that his supplication be accepted. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the aim is constancy in obedience and sincere devotion to God, and al-Tabari cites the report that supplication is worship. Al-Baghawi, al-Sam'ani and al-Nasafi take the same view, while al-Baghawi adds that the phrase may also mean simply "answer my prayer." Al-Razi reads the request as one of seven goals in Abraham's prayer and says it is a plea for acceptance.

Most commentators agree that "some of my descendants" implies only a part. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi say Abraham knew from God that some of his offspring would be unbelievers, while Abu al-Su'ud adds that he could also infer this from the pattern of earlier nations. Ibn 'Ashur disagrees and reads "min" as indicating origin rather than part, arguing that Abraham asks only for the best for himself and his line, and he calls the partitive reading weak.

Opinions differ on the prayer for his parents that follows. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi hold that it was made before Abraham realised that his father was an enemy of God. Al-Zamakhshari suggests it may refer to his mother or to Adam and Eve, while al-Qurtubi reports that some regard his mother as a believer, since God mentioned an excuse only for his father.

Ibrahim asks God to forgive him, his parents and all believers on the Day when the reckoning is established. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi explain that the phrase means the Day when people stand up for their reckoning, the word people being omitted because it is understood. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur see a metaphor instead: the reckoning will be firmly established, as in the expression the war stood on its leg.

The main point of debate concerns the parents. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi hold that Ibrahim prayed for his father before it became clear to him that his father was an enemy of God, as stated in Surah al-Tawba. Al-Baghawi and al-Razi report that his mother may have become a Muslim, and al-Qurtubi finds this not unlikely, citing al-Qushayri. Others, mentioned by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi, say the parents meant are Adam and Eve, or that the prayer was conditional on their embracing Islam. Ibn Juzayy rejects the conditional view and holds that the prayer came before the matter became clear. Ibn al-Anbari adds that Ibrahim prayed while they were still alive, hoping they would be guided.

On the readings, Sa'id ibn Jubayr read the singular, my father, while al-Nakha'i and al-Zuhri read my two sons, meaning Isma'il and Ishaq, as al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi report. As for the believers, Ibn Abbas takes them to be the community of Muhammad, whereas most commentators understand all believers.

The verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ, and through him anyone who might suppose that God is heedless of what the wrongdoers do. God is not unaware of them; He only delays their punishment until a Day when the eyes will stare in terror. Maymun ibn Mihran is quoted as saying the verse is both a warning to the wrongdoer and a consolation to the wronged, a view repeated by al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi offer several readings of the address: a reinforcement of the Prophet in his certainty, a notice that God knows every deed and will hold men to account for the smallest, or a statement that God treats them as a vigilant judge would. Al-Tabari understands the staring eyes as eyes that do not return to their place, while al-Razi reads in them bewilderment and dread. The meaning of 'muhti'in' is debated: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi emphasise hastening towards the summoner, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak take it as a fixed gaze that does not blink, and Ibn Zayd as lowering the head. For 'muqni'i ru'usihim', most take it as raising the heads, though al-Mu'arrij and others read it as bowing them. The most common explanation of 'af'idatuhum hawa' is hearts empty of understanding and good, like a ruined dwelling. Qatada says the hearts have risen into the throats, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that they quiver within the chest.

This passage describes the terror of the Day of Resurrection and the state of the wrongdoers on it. The commentators explain that God is not unaware of what the wrongdoers do, but defers them to a day when eyes will stare in dread. On the word muhti'in, most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, take it to mean hastening towards the summoner, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the sense of a fixed gaze that does not blink, and Ibn Zayd understands it as one who does not lift his head. On muqni'i ru'usihim, the majority, such as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, say it means raising the heads, though al-Mubarrad and some others mention the sense of lowering them, and al-Mubarrad judges raising to be the better known meaning. All agree that their gaze does not return to them. On the hearts being hawa', Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid say they are empty of good and of understanding, a reading al-Tabari adopts. Qatada holds that the hearts have left the chests and lodged in the throats, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr says they churn in the bodies without a place to rest. Commentators support the reading with lines of Hassan and Zuhayr, where the word describes a coward. Several then connect this passage with the account of Nimrod's plot in the following verse, and al-Biqa'i and others read the whole as a picture of overwhelming dread.

The verse tells the Prophet to warn people of the day when punishment will come upon them, which most commentators identify as the Day of Resurrection. The wrongdoers, meaning the polytheists, will then ask their Lord for a short respite so that they may answer His call and follow the messengers, and they will be rebuked for the oath they swore in this world that they would never be removed from it. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid and Qatada, takes the request to be a plea to return to the worldly life to make up for what they neglected, and Ibn Kathir supports this with parallel verses. Al-Mawardi reports two readings of the rebuke: that it means not departing from this world to the hereafter, following Mujahid, or not being relieved of the punishment, following al-Hasan. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur note that the appointed time may refer to the moment of death or to an immediate punishment, while Abu al-Su'ud links it to Judgment Day. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat the oath as either a boastful declaration or one made by the attitude of the people, as their lavish building suggests. On the next verse, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi cite Ali, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid on the scheme of Nimrod, who tried to ascend to heaven, explaining the mention of the mountains. Al-Shawkani gives a further reading that the mountains symbolise the firmness of divine law, and Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi draw a general lesson about the futility of plots against the truth.

This verse reminds the Meccans and others among the Prophet's contemporaries that they had lived in the dwellings of peoples who wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience, such as 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Noah. They had seen, by direct observation and by report, how God destroyed these peoples, and examples had been set out for them in the Quran, so they should have taken warning. The commentators agree that the sense is one of reproach and exhortation, and that on the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoers, when they ask for a respite, are confounded by being reminded that they used to swear they would never be removed, so their request is refused. Qatada and Mujahid take the peoples in question to be all the associationist nations apart from the first. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate the scheming mentioned to the unbelievers' plots against the Prophet, while others, such as Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas according to some reports, recount the story of Nimrod who tried to ascend to heaven in a chest drawn by vultures; Ibn 'Atiyya considered this account unlikely. As for the phrase 'though their scheming were such that the mountains would be moved by it', the readings differ: the majority read with a kasra on the first lam, which gives a negation and a belittling of their scheme, meaning the mountains, a figure for God's religion and laws, stand firm; al-Kisa'i and Ibn Jurayj read with a fatha, which expresses the immensity of their scheme. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn Sa'di stress that the unbelievers harmed God not at all and only harmed themselves, and that the delay is not divine neglect but a respite until a set time.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the scheming of those who wronged themselves through polytheism and the rejection of the messengers. They devised their plot to the utmost of their ability, yet God knows it fully and will requite them for it. As for the phrase "though their scheming could move the mountains", the more common reading, with a kasra on the first lam and a fatha on the second, means that their scheming was not capable of moving anything. Al-Tabari, al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Ashur take this as belittling their plot, with the mountains standing for the firm laws and signs of God, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Razi take the mountains to represent the steadfastness of the Prophet's religion. Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Jurayj read it with a fatha on the first lam and a damma on the second, which magnifies the scale of the scheming to the point that the mountains might have been moved by it. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi record this reading without drawing a firm conclusion from it.

The scholars differ on who the schemers were. Ibn 'Abbas understands the scheming as polytheism, while others think of the Meccans who plotted to kill, imprison or expel the Prophet. Many exegetes report the story of Nimrod who rose into the sky in a chest pulled by vultures, a account that al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya regard as unreliable, though al-Tha'labi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir relate it while noting its weaknesses.

Finally, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi connect the passage to the disbelievers who, having sworn they would never leave this world, now ask for a delay, and they are rebuked for it. The warning to the Prophet not to think that God is heedless is read as consolation for the wronged and a threat to the wrongdoers.

The verse warns the Prophet ﷺ, and through him every reader, not to think that God would break His promise to His messengers to support them and destroy their enemies, for He is mighty and exacts retribution. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the address serves to strengthen the Prophet's resolve, reminding him of what God did to earlier nations that rejected their messengers. The commentators note a grammatical feature: the participle 'breaking' is grammatically linked to 'His promise' while the action falls on the messengers, a usage they illustrate with a line of poetry about a bull and its shadow. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi explain that the promise is placed first to stress that God never breaks His word at all. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi take the promise to mean the victory and help given to the messengers, whereas Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur link it more closely to the punishment of wrongdoers mentioned just before. The reading of the following verse and the meaning of the 'mountains' are debated: Ibn Juzayy and al-Hasan take the mountains to stand for firm divine laws and prophethood, which the schemes of the wicked cannot shake, while others see an exaggeration of how severe their plotting was, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report narratives about Nimrod. Overall the verse affirms God's faithfulness to His word and His power to punish, and several commentators, such as al-Shawkani and King Fahd Complex, note that although addressed to the Prophet it concerns the whole community.

This verse describes the Day of Judgement, when the earth will be changed into another earth and the heavens likewise, and when people will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer. The commentators agree on the general meaning: the creatures will rise from their graves and stand before a Lord whom no power can overcome. They differ on how the change will happen. Ibn Mas'ud says the earth will be replaced by a white land like silver, where no blood has been shed and no sin committed, while Ali ibn Abi Talib says the earth will be silver and the heavens gold. Al-Tabari records other views, including that the earth will become a white loaf of bread from which believers eat beneath their feet, or a fire with Paradise behind it. Ibn Abbas and others hold that it is the same earth whose features are altered: its mountains removed, its valleys levelled, and the sky transformed as the sun is wound up, its stars scattered and the heavens split. Many exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, cite the hadith in which Aisha asks the Prophet where people will be that day and he answers: on the Bridge. Others report that they will be on a white earth like pure bread. Al-Tabari concludes that the soundest reading is that the present earth and heavens will be replaced, without specifying what the replacement will be. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the change may concern attributes or essence, and that the verse allows both readings.

This verse describes the scene of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection, when the earth and the heavens will have been changed and creation will be brought out before God, the One, the Subduer. The criminals are seen bound together in chains. The commentators agree that the 'asfad' are shackles and fetters, but they differ on the meaning of being 'bound together'. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari take it that the hands and feet are drawn up to the neck; al-Kalbi, 'Ata' and Ibn al-Jawzi say each disbeliever is chained to his devil; al-Hasan, Qatada and Abu Hayyan understand that the sinners are grouped with one another according to their deeds and beliefs.

The 'sarabil' are garments, and most exegetes say they are made of tar, the substance used to coat mangy camels because it catches fire quickly. Al-Hasan takes it to be camel tar, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say it is molten copper, relying on a reading that means copper heated to its utmost. The fire then covers their faces, the noblest part of the body. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the purpose is that every soul be repaid for what it earned, and that God is swift in reckoning; Ibn Kathir offers two readings, swiftness of counting or swiftness of settling accounts.

Most commentators link the verse to what precedes it, the divine promise of victory and vengeance, and see in it a warning to wrongdoers and a consolation to the oppressed.

This verse describes the fate of the guilty on the Day of Judgment: they are bound together in chains, their garments are of tar that catches fire quickly, and the fire covers their faces. The commentators agree that the guilty are the disbelievers and polytheists, that the chains (asfad) are shackles and fetters, that the garments (sarabil) are shirts, and that the purpose of this punishment is to repay each soul for what it earned, good or bad. They differ on the meaning of qatran. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada take it to be the tar used to coat camels afflicted with mange, a substance that burns fiercely, while Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to be molten copper, reading the word as qatr an, meaning copper that has reached the peak of its heat. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the gap between these two kinds of tar is like the gap between the two fires. They also differ on 'muqarranin': Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi say each disbeliever is bound with his devil, Ibn Zayd says the hands and feet are drawn up to the neck, and Ibn Qutayba says they are tied to one another. Al-Razi explains that the fire covers the face because it is the noblest outward part of the body and the seat of the senses they did not use to recognise the truth. On the phrase 'the day the earth is changed into another earth', Ibn 'Abbas and most commentators take it as a change of attributes, while Ibn Mas'ud and Ali take it as a change of substance, supported by reports gathered by al-Qurtubi. Finally, the commentators stress that the Qur'an is a message for mankind, so that they may be warned, know that God is One, and that people of understanding may take heed.

The commentators read this verse as the closing description of the terrors of the Day of Judgment: humanity is brought forth before God, the One, the Subduer, and the guilty are seen bound together in shackles, clad in garments of tar, their faces covered by the Fire. The purpose, they agree, is that God recompense every soul for what it has earned, good or evil, and that God is swift in reckoning, meaning no matter distracts Him from another and all creation is, in relation to His power, like a single soul.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the 'asfad' are chains and fetters, with some adding that they are ropes or bonds. Al-Zamakhshari links the phrase in the fetters either to 'muqarranin' or treats it as a state. On the meaning of 'muqarranin', Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi say each disbeliever is chained with his devil, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi allow that the guilty are joined to one another, and Ibn Zayd holds that the hands and feet are drawn up to the neck. Al-Razi lists these views without choosing among them.

On 'qitran', al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada take it to be the tar with which camels are treated; Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to be molten copper, and the reading of 'Ikrima and Ya'qub, 'min qatrin ani', supports this. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that tar catches fire quickly, and al-Razi reads the image as a sign of the soul's suffering while bound to the body.

The commentators agree on the general sense, while differing on lexical details and on the nature of the punishment, and none of them is shown to prevail over the others.

This verse says that the Qur'an is a sufficient message for people, and that it has three aims: that they be warned by it and fear God's punishment, that they know through the proofs it contains that God is one with no partner, and that people of understanding remember and take a lesson from it. Most commentators take the "message" to be the Qur'an, as Ibn Zayd did, while al-Mawardi takes it to mean the warning, and Muqatil identifies the "people" as the inhabitants of Mecca. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that the clause depends on an implied element, and that fear of what is announced leads people to reflect until they reach monotheism, since fear is the mother of all good. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy add that the three aims correspond to two faculties of the soul, knowledge of God and good conduct, and that the verse shows the rank of those who have intellect. Ibn Kathir, al-Tha'alibi and al-Jalalayn stress the reminder as a call to take heed and to change one's ways. Most report that the verse was revealed about Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, according to Yaman ibn Riyab, a report others do not treat as a firm ruling. Ibn Ashur holds that the reference covers the whole surah and that the reminder concerns mainly believers. Al-Shinqiti notes that the Qur'an is a message for all people, and that whoever receives it without believing will be in the Fire.
